name: Aaron Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Aaron. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We've no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the fault crew at the Fenwick depot. Flat country, rivers, lots of willows and poplars, and every one of them wants to fall on a line. Day shift we do planned work, new poles, replacing old fuses, and one week in four I'm on standby at night, so the phone goes and I'm out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same. You know the kit, you know the lads, you know where the bad spans are. What gets to me is the standby week when you get called out three nights running and then do a full day, and the money, because Fenwick's at the bottom of the pay scale and there's nowhere else round here doing this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, at work. I don't really go online, so that's that. With Pete at lunch I'd say they spent all that money and the willows still fall on the lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, which suits me. I know what I'm doing. I'd rather the devil I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up, do the job, take the standby weeks for the extra money. Maybe go fishing a bit more if the rota's kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's the one I'd pick if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the standby money matters. How much of your month is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a busy winter maybe a fifth. In summer hardly anything. Kasia does the school kitchen in term time, so summers are tight, and that's when the car always breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about AI, if this happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Olek's fifteen, he knows more about it than me. I'd tell him the same as my dad told me: learn a trade, keep your head down, turn up on time.

S0.say: I'd say good at work and tell Pete they spent all that money and the willows still fall on the lines. I don't really go online, so that's that.
S0.think: He thinks nothing changing suits him because he knows what he's doing. He'd rather the devil he knows.
S0.do: Carries on turning up, doing the job and taking standby weeks for the extra money. Goes fishing a bit more if the rota allows.
S0.feel: Calm; it's the one he'd pick.
S0.quote: They spent all that money and the willows still fall on the lines.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron speaks in short, plain sentences and doesn't dress anything up. He relies on standby pay, which is seasonal, and summers are the tight months. His advice to his son mirrors his father's almost word for word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one I don't like as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that they'd better train us properly if they change things. I wouldn't make a fuss though. I'm not one for meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me. They already gave the foreman a tablet and half the time he's stood there swearing at it. If my job turns into tapping screens, I'll be the slowest on the crew, and the slowest is who they move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and wait and see what they actually bring in. I'd take every standby week I could get to put a bit by, maybe a couple of hundred over winter. If they make me learn the tablet, I'd ask Olek to show me, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the forecast says maybe storms and you don't know if you'll be called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Olek quietly. Why quietly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want the lads knowing I can't do it. Pete's younger, he picks it up. I'd rather sort it at home where nobody sees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't go to meetings. Would you join the union push if they cut crews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm in the union, I pay my dues. I'd sign whatever they put in front of me. I just wouldn't stand up and talk. Somebody else is better at that.

S1.say: He'd say at work that they'd better train the crew properly if things change. He wouldn't make a fuss, because he's not one for meetings.
S1.think: He worries that if the job turns into tapping screens, he'll be the slowest on the crew, and the slowest gets moved first.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and waits to see what the company brings in. Takes every standby week to save a couple of hundred over winter, and would ask his son to teach him the tablet at home.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a forecast of maybe-storms when you don't know if you'll be called.
S1.quote: If my job turns into tapping screens, I'll be the slowest on the crew, and the slowest is who they move first.
S1.fieldNote: His fear is personal and quiet: being exposed as slow with technology in front of colleagues. He'd learn in private from his teenage son. He supports the union passively but won't speak up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Two years? No.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not say much, to be honest. At work we'd all be stood round the van not knowing what to say. If someone asked I'd say somebody should have seen it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd have nothing. I've done this since I was seventeen. There's no other utility near Fenwick, the warehouse at the ring road is already half machines, and I've got about three weeks of money if the car doesn't go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything I could, first week. Ask Kasia's brother about work at his scrap yard, if that even exists by then. Look at any job going, anything. And we'd probably have to ask Kasia's parents for help with the mortgage, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, really. Like the ground going out from under the bucket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said somebody should have seen it coming. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Government, the companies, I don't know. People who are paid to think about this stuff. I'm not saying one side or the other, they're all the same when it comes to people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zosia, who's eleven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'm not good at that kind of talk. Kasia would do it. I'd probably go out to the shed so they didn't see my face.

S2.say: He'd hardly say anything, with the crew standing round the van not knowing what to say. If asked, he'd say somebody should have seen it coming.
S2.think: Privately he'd feel he has nothing: he's done this since seventeen, there's no other utility near Fenwick, and he has about three weeks of money.
S2.do: Stops all spending he can in the first week and asks his brother-in-law about work at a scrap yard. Applies for any job going and asks his partner's parents for help with the mortgage.
S2.feel: Panicked, like the ground going out from under the bucket.
S2.quote: I'd probably go out to the shed so they didn't see my face.
S2.fieldNote: This picture leaves him with no plan and no words. He blames no side in particular, just people paid to think ahead. Asking his in-laws for money is the thing he dreads most, and he'd still do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five. Still not long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work we'd better get ready, and leave it there. I might go to a union meeting, just to hear what they're saying. I still wouldn't stand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years isn't much better for me. I'm not going to start learning computers at 45. But at least I could see it coming and not get caught on a Tuesday morning with no warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting money aside, even forty a week, and stop the satellite TV. I'd keep doing the job and watch what happens at the bigger depots, see if the robots actually work on poles. If it looked real by year three, maybe I'd get my truck licence, because driving's something I could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd sleep worse, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A truck licence. Wouldn't the robots be driving trucks too, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. I hadn't thought of that. I just know how to drive. I don't know what else there'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said forty a week. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The TV, the takeaway on Fridays, and I'd sell the boat. It's only a little fishing boat. That'd hurt more than the TV.

S3.say: He'd say at work that the crew had better get ready, and leave it there. He might attend a union meeting to listen, but wouldn't stand up.
S3.think: He thinks five years isn't much better because he won't start learning computers at 45. At least he wouldn't get caught with no warning on a Tuesday morning.
S3.do: Saves forty a week by stopping satellite TV and Friday takeaways and selling his small fishing boat. Watches the bigger depots for robot trials and considers a truck licence by year three.
S3.quote: It's only a little fishing boat. That'd hurt more than the TV.
S3.fieldNote: Even with five years he has trouble seeing an exit, and his one idea, driving, falls apart when questioned. Selling the boat is a real sacrifice for him. He waits to see before he moves, even when he's worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be fifty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, at least. I'd tell the lads not to panic. Ten years is a long while in this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the first one where I think I could get somewhere close to the end. The kids would be done with school. I'd still be short of a pension, but closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and put a bit aside every month. I'd wait a few years to see what's real. And I'd make sure Olek and Zosia get a trade or a course that won't vanish, even if it means me doing extra standby to help pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still. But it's a slow kind. I can live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What trade would you push them towards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know anymore, that's the trouble. I used to say electrical. Now I'd ask them what they think, because they'll know better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a few years. Is there a point where waiting is too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. Kasia says I always wait too long. She's right about the boiler and the car, so she's probably right about this.

S4.say: He'd say there's time at least and tell the lads not to panic. Ten years is a long while in this job.
S4.think: Privately ten years is the first picture where he could get close to the end: the kids done with school, and himself closer to pension age though still short.
S4.do: Keeps working, puts a bit aside every month and waits a few years to see what's real. Makes sure his kids get a trade or course that won't vanish, taking extra standby to help pay.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but a slow kind he can live with.
S4.quote: Kasia says I always wait too long. She's right about the boiler and the car, so she's probably right about this.
S4.fieldNote: Time eases him because it gets his children through school, not because he'd change. He admits his habit of waiting too long, through his partner's voice. He no longer knows what trade to recommend, which is new for him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is someone telling me straight what's going to happen and when, and money to tide us over, a year's wages or so, so we don't lose the house. And if there's training, put it on during work hours with someone patient.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No. Maybe how many lads like me there are. Every depot's got two or three. We don't say much, so nobody hears from us.

headlineQuote: Every depot's got two or three. We don't say much, so nobody hears from us.
portrait: Aaron Kowalski is a 43-year-old fault-crew lineworker at a low-paying depot in flat willow country, with a school-kitchen partner, two kids and about three weeks of money. He likes his work because it's the same, and he never uses AI. Mild change makes him quietly worried about being the slowest with screens. The two-year AGI picture leaves him panicked and without a plan, while five years means cuts and waiting, and ten years mostly means getting his kids through school. He doesn't blame any side and won't speak at meetings, but he knows there are many workers like him.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have nothing else to go to near Fenwick and only about three weeks of money.
whatWouldHelp: Straight information on what's happening and when, about a year's wages to keep the house, and patient training during work hours.
